Abstract: We present full-sky maps of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and polarized synchrotron and thermal dust emission, derived from the third set of Planck frequency maps. These products have significantly lower contamination from instrumental systematic effects than previous versions. The methodologies used to derive these maps follow closely those described in earlier papers, adopting four methods ( Commander , NILC , SEVEM , and SMICA ) to extract the CMB component, as well as three methods ( Commander , GNILC , and SMICA ) to extract astrophysical components. Our revised CMB temperature maps agree with corresponding products in the Planck 2015 delivery, whereas the polarization maps exhibit significantly lower large-scale power, reflecting the improved data processing described in companion papers; however, the noise properties of the resulting data products are complicated, and the best available end-to-end simulations exhibit relative biases with respect to the data at the few percent level. Using these maps, we are for the first time able to fit the spectral index of thermal dust independently over 3° regions. We derive a conservative estimate of the mean spectral index of polarized thermal dust emission of β d = 1.55 ± 0.05, where the uncertainty marginalizes both over all known systematic uncertainties and different estimation techniques. For polarized synchrotron emission, we find a mean spectral index of β s = −3.1 ± 0.1, consistent with previously reported measurements. We note that the current data processing does not allow for construction of unbiased single-bolometer maps, and this limits our ability to extract CO emission and correlated components. The foreground results for intensity derived in this paper therefore do not supersede corresponding Planck 2015 products. For polarization the new results supersede the corresponding 2015 products in all respects.

Abstract: The single 248-keV nuclear-recoil candidate reported by LZ is reproduced by dark matter that downscatters, with the relic in the excited state of a pseudo-Dirac pair and a splitting δ\simeq-350\keV. Every interpretation so far advanced is endothermic and places the splitting within a few percent of the xenon kinematic ceiling, so that the predicted count changes from zero to 143 times its central value as the halo escape speed runs from 500 to 600 km/s. The downscattering branch has no threshold speed; the same variation changes its count by 0.3 %. The ratio of counts below 70 keV to those above is 0.011, so the null standard search follows from the kinematics. A weak-strength coupling overproduces the event by 8.9\times10^{5}, so the mediator is a dark-sector one, and longevity of the relic excited state requires |δ|<2m_e. Solving the coupled Boltzmann system removes the one free normalization. Rotating to the eigenchannels of the off-diagonal potential gives σ_0=(π/k^2)\sin^2(δ_+-δ_-), whose phase difference is 0.03 to 1.3 rad, so the Born rate exceeds the s-wave unitarity bound where it is used. One event then requires σ_p\simeq2\times10^{-42} cm^2 and a kinetic mixing ε\simeq1\times10^{-6} at m_{A'}=1\GeV, with beam-dump coverage below 0.6\GeV pushing the mediator above that value. The ground state upscatters endothermically through the same operator, which excludes |δ|\lesssim300 keV and makes the published endothermic reading the small-splitting limit of one model. The decisive test is argon, whose first form-factor zero lies at 695 keV against 94.6 keV for xenon; argon yields 4 to 6 events per tonne-year near 250 keV, where the endothermic reading is forbidden at any exposure.

Abstract: The 2026 LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) high energy nuclear recoil search reports one event at $248\pm23_{\rm stat}\pm23_{\rm sys}~\mathrm{keV}$ and finds the elastic isovector interaction $\mathcal L_6^v$ locally favored at about $3.3σ$ in the heavy dark matter regime. We examine whether this recoil scale can arise from resolved nuclear response within the elastic interaction and compare its spectral, target, and annual modulation behavior with endothermic dark sector excitation. Covariant matching correlates four Galilean operators, removes the longitudinal spin response algebraically, and fixes interference between density and orbital spin orbit amplitudes. The GCN and JJ55 xenon shell model calculations give a second natural xenon cancellation at $211$ and $214~\mathrm{keV}$. In the heavy mass regime, its position changes by less than $0.01~\mathrm{keV}$ from a dark matter mass of $200~\mathrm{GeV}$ to the asymptotic limit. A curvature weighted isotope centroid reproduces the position and residual depth of the natural xenon minimum. Direct $^{40}$Ar calculations shift the nuclear feature to about $350$ and $425~\mathrm{keV}$, whereas endothermic excitation follows reduced mass scaling set by the dark state splitting. At a dark matter mass of $1~\mathrm{TeV}$, the endothermic Ar to Xe scale ratio is $1.082$, compared with $1.63$ to $2.01$ for the nuclear calculations. Elastic scattering gives a few percent annual modulation in the adopted halo model, while endothermic solutions near the maximum laboratory halo speed show much larger seasonal variation. These scaling and timing behaviors provide tests of a target-dependent nuclear cancellation against an excitation energy set by dark sector kinematics.

Abstract: The 2026 LUX-ZEPLIN search reports one nuclear recoil candidate at $248\pm23_{\rm stat}\pm23_{\rm sys}~\mathrm{keV}$ in an extended window reaching about $270~\mathrm{keV}$. The nonrelativistic reduction correlates $\mathcal O_{17}$ and $\mathcal O_{20}$, relating a coherent charge branch to a transverse spin tensor branch. For $m_X=1~\mathrm{TeV}$, natural xenon exhibits a broad high recoil maximum at $204.8$ to $206.6~\mathrm{keV}$ and retains $80.4$ to $85.4\%$ of this maximum at $248~\mathrm{keV}$. Resolving the interaction through a dark photon relates the high-to-low recoil ratio to the mediator mass. A renormalizable $SU(2)_X\times U(1)_D$ realization stabilizes the complex vector by a residual $Z_3$ gauge symmetry and generates the toroidal current through vectorlike messengers carrying a physical CP phase. For a benchmark with $m_X=0.998~\mathrm{TeV}$ and $m_{A'}=0.450~\mathrm{GeV}$, $R(248)/R(50)=1.43$ for GCN and $1.21$ for JJ55, while the odd $A$ xenon fraction remains above $99.9\%$. The response level ratio between the $350$ to $590~\mathrm{keV}$ and $100$ to $270~\mathrm{keV}$ intervals is about $0.46$ at this benchmark. The tensor branch is absent for spin zero argon, whereas annual modulation remains at the few percent level. The resulting spectral, isotope, target, timing, mediator, and high energy dependences give correlated tests of an elastic tensor interpretation of the LZ recoil.

Abstract: The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment has reported a single candidate event in the high-energy nuclear recoil window $248\pm32.5\ \mathrm{keV}_{\mathrm{nr}}$ with an exposure of $2.84\ \mathrm{ton}\cdot\mathrm{yr}$, while the low-energy spectrum remains consistent with background expectations. For a dark matter mass $m_χ\simeq 247\ \mathrm{MeV}$, the coherent absorption process produces a monoenergetic nuclear recoil at $E_R \simeq 248\ \mathrm{keV}_{\mathrm{nr}}$. The required single-nucleon absorption cross section is $σ_{χN}^{\mathrm{NC}} = 1.07\times10^{-46}\ \mathrm{cm}^2$, corresponding to an effective field theory scale $Λ\simeq 11.5\ \mathrm{TeV}$. However, a recasting analysis of KamLAND data on the neutron-emission channel $χ+{}^{12}\mathrm{C} \to ν+ n + {}^{11}\mathrm{C}^*$ excludes this benchmark parameter space, establishing a significant tension between the LZ excess interpretation and existing constraints from large-volume scintillator detectors. Abstract: Higgsino dark matter (DM) is considered one of the most well-motivated and minimal DM scenarios arising from supersymmetric extensions of the Standard Model. Motivated by the requirement of electroweak naturalness, Higgsinos are expected to be relatively light, with masses close to the weak scale. While a pure Higgsino state typically evades current direct detection limits, next-to-leading (NLO) order radiative corrections may bring it within the sensitivity of upcoming experiments. On the contrary, a more important consequence, observed specifically near the kinematic threshold for the production of two particles, is that the NLO corrections lower the DM-nucleon cross section below the neutrino floor. We find that the mass of the winolike ${\ensuremath{\chi}}_{2}^{0}$ can be probed up to about 310 (230) GeV at $2\ensuremath{\sigma}$ ($5\ensuremath{\sigma}$) level for an integrated luminosity $\mathcal{L}=300\text{ }\text{ }{\mathrm{fb}}^{\ensuremath{-}1}$. In the future HL-LHC with $3000\text{ }\text{ }{\mathrm{fb}}^{\ensuremath{-}1}$ luminosity, the corresponding mass limits can be pushed up to 430 (330) GeV.

arXiv ID: 2403.19598
Title: Implications of purity constraints on light Higgsinos
Authors: Stephen P. Martin
Categories: Particle physics theoretical and experimental studies
Published: 2024-05-30
DOI: 10.1103/physrevd.109.095045
URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19598
PDF URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.19598
Abstract: The lightest supersymmetric particles could be Higgsinos that have a small mixing with gauginos. If the lightest Higgsino-like state makes up some or all of the dark matter with a thermal freeze-out density, then its mass must be between about 100 GeV and 1150 GeV, and dark matter searches put bounds on the amount of gaugino contamination that it can have. Motivated by the generally good agreement of flavor- and C P -violating observables with Standard Model predictions, I consider models in which the scalar particles of minimal supersymmetry are heavy enough to be essentially decoupled, except for the 125 GeV Higgs boson. I survey the resulting purity constraints as lower bounds on the gaugino masses and upper bounds on the Higgsino mass splittings. I also discuss the mild excesses in recent soft lepton searches for charginos and neutralinos at the LHC, and show that they can be accommodated in these models if tan β is small and μ is negative. Published by the American Physical Society 2024

Abstract: Abstract This report describes the experimental strategy and technologies for XLZD, the next-generation xenon observatory sensitive to dark matter and neutrino physics. In the baseline design, the detector will have an active liquid xenon target of 60 tonnes, which could be increased to 80 tonnes if the market conditions for xenon are favorable. It is based on the mature liquid xenon time projection chamber technology used in current-generation experiments, LZ and XENONnT. The report discusses the baseline design and opportunities for further optimization of the individual detector components. The experiment envisaged here has the capability to explore parameter space for Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP) dark matter down to the neutrino fog, with a 3 $$\sigma $$ σ evidence potential for WIMP-nucleon cross sections as low as $$3\times 10^{-49}\mathrm \,cm^2$$ 3 × 10 - 49 c m 2 (at 40 GeV/c $$^2$$ 2 WIMP mass). The observatory will also have leading sensitivity to a wide range of alternative dark matter models. It is projected to have a 3 $$\sigma $$ σ observation potential of neutrinoless double beta decay of $$^{136}$$ 136 Xe at a half-life of up to $$5.7\times 10^{27}$$ 5.7 × 10 27 years. Additionally, it is sensitive to astrophysical neutrinos from the sun and galactic supernovae.

issues.text: The (794/776)^2 rescaling of delta(N=1) and delta(N=0.3) from 352.5/356.4 keV to about 369/373 keV is a heuristic. It assumes the whole N(delta) curve stretches with v_max^2, but near the kinematic edge the count depends on how the halo tail is populated between v_min and v_max, not only on where the edge sits. The arithmetic checks out (mu = 109.8 GeV gives delta_max = 367.8 and 385 keV), but the shifted window has not been computed. The claim that 2609.02608 uses v_max = 794 km/s is also unsourced, so attributing 17 keV of the 24.5 keV offset to the cutoff is an assumption.

The 350 keV point (N = 1.97, peak E_R = 315 keV) and the 300 keV point (744.6) come from wave-1 calls under d-02 and are not among this finding's evidence ids. The interpolations check out: ln-linear between 1.97 and 0.494 gives 352.45 keV, and between 0.494 and 0.085 gives 356.4 keV. The finding should still cite the d-02 call ids for the 350 keV anchor.

The board brief still says 'I did not compute any relic densities... No inelastic-DM or relic-density tools were available'. This contradicts d-01, which computed Omega h^2 at five masses (crossing at about 1158 GeV), and d-02 and d-05, which computed LZ event counts. The brief must be rewritten before synthesis. # The thermal higgsino at 1.0–1.2 TeV: relic target, xenon reach and current limits

## Abstract

This investigation asked where the thermal higgsino (about 1.0–1.2 TeV) sits relative to the Planck abundance and to current direct- and indirect-detection limits. The context is the 2026 LZ extended-window result, which reported one nuclear-recoil candidate at 248 keV.

An inelastic-DM tool server was used for relic densities and for LZ event counts. Its relic calculation is a single-channel freeze-out scaling, not a Sommerfeld/coannihilation calculation. It reaches Omega h^2 = 0.120 at about 1158 GeV, inside the literature range of 1.08–1.2 TeV.

For a 1.1 TeV higgsino with Z-mediated inelastic scattering, the tool predicts:
- hundreds of LZ events at a splitting of delta = 300 keV;
- about 1 event at delta ≈ 352.5 keV;
- essentially none above about 365–370 keV.

The cutoff at high splitting comes from the kinematic edge delta_max = mu v_max^2 / 2, which is about 368 keV for the tool's 776 km/s halo cutoff and about 385 keV for 794 km/s.

The literature bound from solar-capture neutrinos (delta > 566 keV) is quoted from a 2026 paper whose abstract text was not retrieved. If that bound holds, every thermal higgsino allowed by solar capture lies beyond LZ's inelastic reach under the Standard Halo Model. Its elastic loop-level rate is quoted in the literature as lying below the neutrino floor, though no number was sourced.

Abstract-level literature indicates that current gamma-ray line searches do not exclude the thermal higgsino, with the conclusion depending on the halo profile. CTAO is identified as the decisive future test.

Conclusion: the full-abundance thermal higgsino is not excluded. Its sub-MeV-splitting interpretation of the LZ event is in tension with solar capture and with the empty sideband.

Two caveats apply throughout. All 2026-dated arXiv IDs were found through an OpenAlex-backed search, and none could be verified on arxiv.org. No citation could be va

while arXiv:2609.06760 quotes 0.51–0.56 MeV. Two further tensions are reported:
- the empty sideband above 350 keV disfavours the thermal-mass fit (arXiv:2609.09385, arXiv:2609.26698);
- halo uncertainties are not sufficient to reconcile the higgsino with solar capture (arXiv:2609.15321).

A Planck-compatible branch survives at delta ≈ 0.85–1.34 MeV (arXiv:2610.00226). arXiv:2609.09136 proposes a non-higgsino alternative.

All 2609.x and 2610.x IDs came through OpenAlex and are unverified.

## Results

### Relic density from the tool

`compute_relic_density` was run with the higgsino setting enabled. The results are below; the tension column is as reported by the tool against Planck 0.120 ± 0.0012.

| m_chi (GeV) | sigma_v (cm^3/s) | Omega h^2 | Tension (as reported) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 900 | 3.73e-26 | 0.0731 | 39.1σ |
| 1000 | 3.03e-26 | 0.0898 | 25.1σ |
| 1100 | 2.5e-26 | 0.1083 | 9.8σ |
| 1200 | 2.10e-26 | 0.1285 | 7.1σ |
| 1300 | 1.79e-26 | 0.1503 | 25.2σ |

Linear interpolation crosses 0.120 at about 1158 GeV, with ±6 GeV from the ±0.0012 band (about ±5 GeV for a ±0.001 band). A direct call at 1159 GeV returns 0.120.

This crossing lies inside the 1.08–1.2 TeV literature range. It sits about 60–80 GeV above the 1.08–1.1 TeV values and close to the about 1.2 TeV value of arXiv:2410.15733.

The tool's physics is limited:
- It uses a fixed scaling sigma_v = 2.5e-26 cm^3/s × (1100 GeV/m)^2.
- It feeds this into a Kolb–Turner freeze-out estimate (x_f ≈ 24.4–24.8, g* = 86.25).
- It has no Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch.

The crossing therefore reflects how the tool was calibrated rather than a higgsino calculation. The planned with/without-Sommerfeld comparison could not be run.

The tool's Planck consistency flag also returns True at 7–25σ tension, which appears to be a bug.

### Inelastic LZ event counts and xenon's kinematic reach

The tool's `predict_recoil` uses the following setup:
- Z-exchange higgsino with sigma_n = 7.43e-39 cm^2;
- the LZ 2.84 t-yr

extended nuclear-recoil window;
- a hard halo cutoff at v_esc + v_E = 776 km/s.

At m_chi = 1100 GeV it gives:

| delta (keV) | N_LZ | Peak E_R (keV) | v_min for the 248 keV event (km/s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 300 | 744.6 | 270 | 701 |
| 350 | 1.97 (P(N≥1) = 0.86) | 315 | 762 |
| 355 | 0.494 | 320 | 768 |
| 360 | 0.085 | 324 | 774 |
| 365 | 0.009 | 329 | 781 (inaccessible) |
| 370 | 0.00 | 333 | 787 |
| 375 | 0.00 | 338 | 793 |
| 380 | 0.00 | 342 | 799 |
| 500 | 0.00 | 450 | 945 |
| 566 | 0.00 | 510 | 1025 |
| 700 | 0.00 | 630 | 1189 |

Log-linear interpolation gives delta(N=1) = 352.5 keV and delta(N=0.3) = 356.4 keV. The one-event window is therefore only about 4 keV wide: N falls by a factor of about 4–6 per 5 keV.

The mass dependence is weak:
- At 1159 GeV, the tool's own thermal mass, delta = 360 keV gives N = 0.135, compared with 0.085 at 1100 GeV. This raises delta(N=1) by about 1–2 keV.
- At delta = 380 keV, the 248 keV event needs v_min = 802, 799 and 796 km/s at m = 1000, 1100 and 1200 GeV. All exceed the cutoff.

The kinematic edge can be worked by hand. Taking m_Xe ≈ 122 GeV and m_chi = 1100 GeV gives mu = 109.8 GeV. Then delta_max = mu v_max^2 / 2 is about 368 keV for v_max = 776 km/s (beta^2 = 6.70e-6) and about 385 keV for 544 + 250 = 794 km/s. This matches the tool's transition between 350 and 380 keV. It also shows that the 0 events above 370 keV are caused by the hard 776 km/s cutoff, not by the energy window.

At 1.1 TeV the tool therefore divides the splitting axis into three regions:
- below about 340 keV, excluded (hundreds of events);
- about 345–368 keV, able to produce the 248 keV event;
- above about 370 keV, beyond xenon's reach.

The literature's solar-capture bound (> 566 keV) and the LMC-preferred 480–520 keV both lie above even the 385 keV edge obtained with v_max = 794 km/s.

The halo cutoff could not be varied, because `predict_recoil` takes no halo parameters. Rescaling by (794/776)^2 = 1.047 moves delta(N=1) and delta(N=0.3) to abo

ut 369 and 373 keV. This is a heuristic that has not been computed, and it assumes the whole N(delta) curve stretches with the edge. Near the edge, the count actually depends on how the velocity tail is populated.

Comparison with the literature fits:
- **350 keV** (arXiv:2609.01504) agrees directly with the tool.
- **377 keV** (arXiv:2609.02608): the 776 versus 794 km/s cutoff could account for about 17 keV of the 24.5 keV offset. That attribution is an assumption, because the cutoff used by that paper is unsourced. The remaining 5–8 keV is unexplained.
- **339 keV** (arXiv:2609.26698) is an optimum of sideband ratios and does not depend on the overall rate. It is not comparable with the tool's absolute count, which is far above one event at that splitting.

### Annual modulation

At 1100 GeV, 350 keV and E_R = 248 keV, the tool gives a 98.5% fractional modulation peaking on June 2. On the event date of September 1, the rate is 22.5% of the peak.

### Parameter-plane scan

A 17×17 scan over m_chi = 800–1400 GeV and delta = 0–800 keV produced the file `scan_idm.npz`. The tool reports 144 of 289 points as passing all constraints, with 9 points predicting 0.3–5 LZ events. The best fit is at m_chi = 988 GeV, delta = 350 keV, and a summary plot was written to `constraint_summary.png`. A recoil-spectrum plot for 1100 GeV and 380 keV is at `recoil_spectrum.png`. All files are under `/Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/`.

The viable count should not be read as physics, for two reasons:
- It inherits the faulty relic "passes" flag.
- It uses an indirect-detection model that treats annihilation as p-wave and suppressed by the mass splitting.

The best fit is also a fit to the LZ event, not to the relic abundance. By the tool's own relic curve, 988 GeV gives Omega h^2 ≈ 0.087, which is under-abundant.

### Combined constraint check

`check_all_constraints` returned VIABLE at four points: 1100 GeV with delta = 400, 566 and 1000 keV, and 1159 GeV

with delta = 400 keV. At all four it gives N_LZ = 0.00 and no Fermi-LAT or CMB exclusion.

Its present-day sigma_v is about 7e-42 to 5e-41 cm^3/s, labelled "p-wave + mass-splitting suppressed". This is far below the s-wave higgsino value of about 1e-26 cm^3/s. The indirect-detection part of this check is therefore physically inappropriate and has been replaced by the literature assessment below.

### Elastic leg (literature only)

The XENONnT 3.1 t-yr search (arXiv:2502.18005) reaches a minimum spin-independent limit of 1.7e-47 cm^2 at 30 GeV (90% CL), with best median sensitivity 1.4e-47 cm^2 at 41 GeV. The 1.09 t-yr result (arXiv:2303.14729) reached 2.58e-47 cm^2 at 28 GeV.

Neither abstract gives the limit at 1 TeV. The figure of about 1e-45 cm^2 at 1 TeV is only an extrapolation from linear high-mass scaling.

The loop-level pure-higgsino cross section of about 1e-48 to 1e-49 cm^2 is not sourced. arXiv:2607.20588 states qualitatively that it lies below the neutrino floor. For scale, XLZD (arXiv:2410.17137) projects 3σ evidence potential down to 3e-49 cm^2 at 40 GeV.

### Indirect detection (literature, abstracts only)

- **Fermi-LAT.** arXiv:2405.13104 ran a 15-year Fermi-LAT line-like search that comes "within an order one factor" of higgsino sensitivity for some Milky Way analog profiles. In the same analysis H.E.S.S. is subleading to Fermi.
- **Current IACTs.** arXiv:2210.03140 finds the higgsino "out of reach by at least a factor of a few" even at the ultimate sensitivity of H.E.S.S.-like instruments. Its dominant systematic is the inner-Galaxy dark matter distribution.
- **H.E.S.S. Inner Galaxy Survey.** The 2026-dated, unverified arXiv:2608.07234 (546 h) quotes a line limit of 2.3e-28 cm^3/s at 1 TeV for an Einasto profile. It says thermal higgsinos are "probed" for the first time, but its abstract does not say whether, or for which profiles, they are excluded.
- **Future instruments.** CTA could be the first experiment sensitive to the thermal higgsino (a

rXiv:2008.00692). CTA and SWGO could detect it at high significance for all but the most pessimistic profiles (arXiv:2405.13104). CTAO-North could reach the required sensitivity within a decade (arXiv:2506.08084).

No MAGIC-specific higgsino limit was found. The literature assessments of the thermal target relative to current reach (items above) have not been independently verified: they rest on abstract text that could not be validated.

## Discussion

The answer to "where does the higgsino sit" has three parts.

**Relic.** The full-abundance target is about 1.1–1.2 TeV. The tool's crossing at about 1158 GeV is consistent with this, but only because of how the tool is calibrated.

**Direct detection.** Two independent constraints combine:
- xenon's kinematic edge, about 368–385 keV at 1.1 TeV depending on the velocity cutoff;
- the reported solar-capture lower bound on delta (566 keV, or 0.51–0.56 MeV in an independent analysis).

Together they leave no Standard-Halo-Model splitting at which a thermal higgsino both produces LZ events and survives solar capture. The tool reproduces the one-event splitting near 350 keV. It also shows how narrow and cutoff-dependent that window is, which explains why the literature fits scatter between 339 and 377 keV. The LMC-tail interpretation (481–519 keV) moves the window upward, but it still falls short of 566 keV. This is consistent with the conclusion of arXiv:2609.15321 that halo uncertainties cannot close the gap.

At MeV-scale splittings, which arXiv:2610.00226 reports as allowed, inelastic xenon searches have no reach. The elastic rate is stated to lie below the neutrino floor, although no number was sourced here.

**Indirect detection.** On the abstract-level evidence, the thermal higgsino is not excluded. It lies within a factor of order one of Fermi-LAT line sensitivity for favourable profiles, and CTAO is the decisive test.

**Tensions.** The roughly 5–8 keV of the offset from the 377 keV fit remains unexplained. The t

ool's mass crossing sits 60–80 GeV above the 1.08–1.1 TeV values used in the 2026 papers.

**Dead ends.** Two attempts were made to obtain verbatim citations: the Planck 2018 parameters paper (1807.06209), arXiv:2410.15733, arXiv:2609.02823 and arXiv:2609.02775. Every arXiv-API-backed tool (metadata lookup, two download tools, and `cite`'s metadata check) failed. They returned "not found" even for the long-established Planck ID, or HTTP 429, timeouts, or an internal error ("'Search' object has no attribute 'results'"). A "not found" result therefore carries no information about whether a paper exists. Only OpenAlex abstracts were reachable.

The planned Sommerfeld comparison and the halo-sensitivity scan were not possible, because the relic and recoil tools expose no such parameters.

## Limitations

- **Relic calculation.** No genuine Sommerfeld or coannihilation calculation was performed. The tool is a toy scaling calibrated near 1.1 TeV, and its Planck consistency flags are unreliable.
- **Halo dependence.** Not computed. The 369/373 keV shift under a 794 km/s cutoff is a heuristic, and no smooth-tail or LMC halo was modelled.
- **Energy binning.** Binned counts in the [14,225), [225,271] and (271,800] keV windows, and the sideband analysis of arXiv:2609.26698, were not reproduced. The tool returns integrated counts only.
- **LZ implementation.** It is unconfirmed whether the tool's LZ implementation matches the published 2026 efficiencies, and XENONnT does not appear to be implemented.
- **Unsourced numbers.** These include the Planck value Omega_c h^2 = 0.120 ± 0.001, the 1 TeV elastic limit, and the loop-level higgsino cross section.
- **Solar-capture bound.** The bound of delta > 566 keV carries the bottom line, yet no abstract excerpt containing it was retrieved.
- **2026 IDs.** None of the 2026-dated IDs (2606–2610) were verified on arxiv.org, and no quote passed `cite()`.
- **Indirect detection.** The indirect-detection status rests on abstracts, and the p

redicted line cross section relative to the limit could not be extracted.
- **Budget.** Both planned waves were used.

1. Verify that the 2026-dated arXiv IDs resolve, and retrieve abstract-level text for the solar-capture bound of delta > 566 keV (arXiv:2609.02775, 2609.06760, 2609.15321, 2610.00226), since the bottom line depends on it.
2. Compute the inelastic LZ count with a configurable halo (v_esc = 544 km/s, smooth truncated Maxwellian, LMC tail) to test the 369/373 keV heuristic and explain the residual 5–8 keV offset from the 377 keV fit.
3. Run a genuine pure-higgsino relic calculation with Sommerfeld enhancement and chargino coannihilation, to replace the toy cr

# The 1.0–1.2 TeV thermal higgsino against LZ, XENONnT, Planck and gamma-ray limits: toy-model calculations and an abstract-level literature survey

## Abstract

This investigation asked where the pure higgsino thermal relic, at about 1.0–1.2 TeV, sits relative to current limits.

**Tool calculations.** An inelastic-dark-matter (inelastic-DM) server was used for relic and recoil calculations.

- **Relic density.** The server's relic model is a single-channel freeze-out scaling calibrated near 1.1 TeV. It reaches the Planck abundance at about 1158 GeV. This lies inside the 1.08–1.2 TeV literature range, but it is a calibration result, not a Sommerfeld/coannihilation prediction.
- **LZ inelastic events.** The server's Z-exchange higgsino predicts these LZ counts at 1.1 TeV for the 2.84 tonne-year extended nuclear-recoil window:

| Mass splitting delta (keV) | Expected LZ events |
|---|---|
| 300 | 744.6 (excluded) |
| 350 | about 2 |
| 380 and above | 0 |

- **Kinematic edge and one-event window.** The cutoff sits at about 368 keV for the tool's 776 km/s halo cutoff. It would sit at about 385 keV for 794 km/s. The "about one event" window is only about 4 keV wide, at 352–356 keV.

**Literature, from abstracts only.** None of the following could be verified against full texts.

- Solar-capture limits from IceCube require delta > 566 keV.
- That puts every solar-capture-allowed thermal higgsino beyond the inelastic reach of xenon.
- The pure-higgsino elastic cross section is described as lying below the neutrino floor.
- The higgsino is not excluded by current gamma-ray line searches, and the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO) is identified as the decisive future test.

**Bottom line.** The full-abundance thermal higgsino at about 1.1 TeV is not excluded. Its interpretation as the source of the sub-MeV-splitting LZ 248 keV event is disfavoured. With splittings of order an MeV it is effectively invisible to current xenon detectors.

## Background

**Thermal mass.** With Sommerfeld enhancement and coannihilation included, a pure higgsino gives the full Planck abundance at roughly 1.0–1.2 TeV. Quoted values are:

- about 1.08–1.1 TeV (arXiv:2609.02775, arXiv:2609.02608);
- "~1.2 TeV" (arXiv:2410.15733);
- an upper end of about 1150 GeV, with the thermal higgsino-like mass required to lie "between about 100 GeV and 1150 GeV" (arXiv:2403.19598).

Lighter thermal higgsinos are under-abundant by a factor of 5–20 in natural SUSY (arXiv:1803.11210).

**Direct detection.** The pure higgsino is inelastic dark matter. Z-mediated scattering requires the neutral-state splitting delta to be no more than a few hundred keV. If delta lies beyond the kinematic reach of xenon, only loop-level elastic scattering remains, and that rate sits near or below the neutrino fog (arXiv:2609.01504, arXiv:2410.02723). One 2026 abstract states that next-to-leading-order corrections push the pure-higgsino nucleon cross section "below the neutrino floor" (arXiv:2607.20588). Higgsino–gaugino mixing raises the elastic rate (arXiv:2606.31013).

**The 2026 LZ result.** LZ reported a 2.84 tonne-year search with a recoil window extended to about 270 keV (arXiv:2609.02823). It found one event at 248 ± 23 (stat) ± 23 (sys) keV, with 2.6σ global and 3.4σ local significance.

Interpretations of that event as a higgsino give these preferred splittings:

| Assumption or method | Preferred delta | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Standard Halo Model | about 350 keV | arXiv:2609.01504 |
| Standard Halo Model | 377 keV | arXiv:2609.02608 |
| Sideband optimum at 1 TeV | 339 keV, about 1.9σ tension | arXiv:2609.26698 |
| Including the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) | about 480–520 keV | arXiv:2609.01504; 481–519 keV in arXiv:2609.01590 |

**Tensions with the event interpretation.**

- **Solar capture.** IceCube non-observation requires delta > 566 keV (arXiv:2609.02775). This is supported by arXiv:2609.11833 and arXiv:2609.07807. arXiv:2609.06760 quotes 0.51–0.56 MeV.
- **Empty sideband.** The absence of events above 350 keV is in tension with the thermal-mass fit (arXiv:2609.09385, arXiv:2609.26698).
- **Halo uncertainties.** These cannot close the gap (arXiv:2609.15321). Under the Standard Halo Model, delta > 566 keV would need v0 > 240 km/s. With the LMC included, the largest workable splitting is 514 keV.

**Surviving branch.** A Planck-compatible thermal branch survives at delta of about 0.85–1.34 MeV (arXiv:2610.00226). arXiv:2609.09136 proposes a non-higgsino alternative.

**Caveat on sources.** All 2026-dated identifiers came from an OpenAlex-backed search and could not be resolved through the arXiv API. They should be checked on arxiv.org before anyone cites them.

## Results

### Relic density from the inelastic-DM server (toy model)

The relic tool was run with the higgsino flag set. This flag sets σv = 2.5×10⁻²⁶ cm³/s × (1100 GeV/m)² and feeds it into a Kolb–Turner freeze-out estimate, with x_f about 24.5 and g* = 86.25. The tool has no Sommerfeld or coannihilation switch.

| m_χ (GeV) | Ω h² |
|---|---|
| 900 | 0.0731 |
| 1000 | 0.0898 |
| 1100 | 0.1083 |
| 1200 | 0.1285 |
| 1300 | 0.1503 |

- **Planck crossing.** Linear interpolation reaches Ω h² = 0.120 at about 1158 GeV. The server's ±0.0012 band gives ±6 GeV; the ±0.001 band gives about ±5 GeV. A direct call at 1159 GeV returns 0.120.
- **Comparison with the literature.** This crossing is inside the 1.08–1.2 TeV range. It is about 60–80 GeV above the 1.08–1.1 TeV values and close to the ~1.2 TeV value of arXiv:2410.15733.
- **Interpretation.** The agreement reflects how the tool's cross section is normalized. It should be read as a toy-model crossing, not a higgsino prediction.
- **Tests not run.** The with/without-Sommerfeld comparison and splitting-dependence tests could not be done.
- **Pass flag.** The tool marks results as "consistent" with Planck even at 7–25σ tension; for example, 1100 GeV carries 9.8σ tension. This looks like a bug.

### LZ inelastic event counts and the kinematic reach of xenon

The recoil tool uses:

- Z exchange, with σ_n = 7.43×10⁻³⁹ cm² per nucleon;
- the LZ 2.84 tonne-year extended nuclear-recoil window;
- a hard halo cutoff at v_esc + v_E = 776 km/s.

Expected LZ counts at m_χ = 1100 GeV:

| delta (keV) | Expected LZ events | Spectrum peak (keV) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 300 | 744.6 | not recorded | Grossly excluded against 1 observed event |
| 350 | 1.97 | 315 | P(N ≥ 1) = 0.86; the 248 keV event needs v_min = 762 km/s, which is accessible |
| 380 | 0.00 | 342 | The 248 keV event needs v_min = 799 km/s, which is inaccessible |
| 500 | 0.00 | 450 | |
| 566 | 0.00 | 510 | |
| 700 | 0.00 | 630 | |

**Hand check of the edge.** The maximum splitting is δ_max = μ v_max²/2. With m_Xe of about 122 GeV, the reduced mass is μ = 109.8 GeV.

- For v_max = 776 km/s, δ_max is about 368 keV.
- For v_max = 794 km/s (544 + 250 km/s), δ_max is about 385 keV.

This matches the tool, which gives events at 350 keV and none at 380 keV.

**Mass dependence.** The edge depends only weakly on mass. At delta = 380 keV, v_min for the 248 keV event is 802, 799 and 796 km/s at 1000, 1100 and 1200 GeV, all above 776 km/s.

**Consequence.** The solar-capture bound of delta > 566 keV from the literature therefore puts every solar-capture-allowed thermal higgsino beyond LZ's inelastic reach under the Standard Halo Model.

**Annual modulation.** At 1100 GeV, 350 keV and E_R = 248 keV, the tool gives:
- a fractional amplitude of 98.5%, peaking on June 2;
- 22.5% of the peak rate on the event date of September 1.

A recoil-spectrum plot for 1100 GeV and 380 keV was written to `/Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/recoil_spectrum.png`. No numbered figure was produced for this report.

### The one-event splitting window

A finer scan at 1100 GeV gives:

| delta (keV) | Expected LZ events | Spectrum peak (keV) |
|---|---|---|
| 350 | 1.97 | 315 |
| 355 | 0.494 | 320 |
| 360 | 0.085 | 324 |
| 365 | 0.009 | 329 |
| 370 | 0.00 | 333 |
| 375 | 0.00 | 338 |

- **Window location.** Log-linear interpolation gives delta(N=1) = 352.5 keV and delta(N=0.3) = 356.4 keV. The window is therefore about 4 keV wide, and N falls by about 4–6 times per 5 keV.
- **Where the event becomes inaccessible.** The 248 keV event drops out between 360 and 365 keV, where v_min rises from 774 to 781 km/s.
- **Thermal mass.** At the tool's thermal mass of 1159 GeV, delta = 360 keV gives N = 0.135, against 0.085 at 1100 GeV. This moves delta(N=1) up by only about 1–2 keV.
- **Cause of the zero counts.** The zero counts at delta ≥ 370 keV come from the hard 776 km/s cutoff, not the energy window.
- **Halo dependence (not computed).** The recoil tool has no halo inputs, so halo dependence could not be computed. An analytic rescaling by (794/776)² = 1.047 would move the window to about 369–373 keV. This is a heuristic: near the edge, the count depends on how the velocity tail is populated, not only on where the edge sits.

Comparison with literature fits:

- **350 keV (arXiv:2609.01504).** Agrees with the tool directly.
- **377 keV (arXiv:2609.02608).** The offset is 24.5 keV. About 17 keV of it would be explained if that paper used a 794 km/s cutoff, but this is an assumption, not a sourced fact. The remaining roughly 5–8 keV is unexplained. Possible causes are the halo tail shape, v_E at the event date, and cross-section or efficiency normalization; none was tested.
- **339 keV (arXiv:2609.26698).** This is a normalization-free sideband-ratio optimum. With the tool's normalization, splittings this low give hundreds of events, so it is not a like-for-like comparison.

The tool therefore does not by itself account for the spread among literature fits.

### Parameter scan and constraint checker

A 17 × 17 scan covered m_χ = 800–1400 GeV and delta = 0–800 keV. It reported 144 of 289 points "viable" and 9 points predicting 0.3–5 LZ events. The best-fit point is m_χ = 988 GeV, delta = 350 keV. Output files are:

- `/Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/scan_idm.npz`
- `/Users/nramachandra/github-integration/inelastic-dm-server/output/constraint_summary.png`

These numbers should not be taken as physics, for three reasons:

- The viable count uses the relic pass flag that stays true at 7–25σ.
- It uses an indirect-detection model that is wrong for a higgsino (see below).
- The best fit fits the LZ event, not the relic. At 988 GeV the tool's own relic curve gives Ω h² of about 0.087, so this point is under-abundant.

The constraint checker rated four points VIABLE: 1100 GeV with delta = 400, 566 and 1000 keV, and 1159 GeV with 400 keV. All four have N_LZ = 0.00 and no Fermi-LAT or CMB exclusion. Its present-day σv of about 7×10⁻⁴² to 5×10⁻⁴¹ cm³/s is labelled "p-wave + mass-splitting suppressed". That is inappropriate for an s-wave, Sommerfeld-enhanced higgsino, whose cross section is about 10⁻²⁶ cm³/s.

### Elastic scattering (literature only)

The XENONnT 3.1 tonne-year search (arXiv:2502.18005) reports:
- a minimum spin-independent limit of 1.7×10⁻⁴⁷ cm² at 30 GeV (90% CL);
- a best median sensitivity of 1.4×10⁻⁴⁷ cm² at 41 GeV.

The earlier 1.09 tonne-year result (arXiv:2303.14729) reached 2.58×10⁻⁴⁷ cm² at 28 GeV.

Neither abstract gives the limit at 1 TeV. The figure of about 10⁻⁴⁵ cm² is only an extrapolation using linear high-mass scaling.

XLZD (arXiv:2410.17137) reaches the neutrino fog, with 3σ evidence potential down to 3×10⁻⁴⁹ cm² at 40 GeV.

The pure-higgsino loop-level elastic cross section of about 10⁻⁴⁸–10⁻⁴⁹ cm² was not sourced. arXiv:2607.20588 places it qualitatively below the neutrino floor without giving a number.

### Indirect detection (literature only)

These findings are based on abstracts only. The full text of arXiv:2405.13104 could not be downloaded.

- **Fermi-LAT.** A 15-year line-like search comes "within an order one factor" of the sensitivity needed to detect the higgsino, for some simulated Milky Way profiles. In the same analysis, H.E.S.S. is subleading to Fermi (arXiv:2405.13104).
- **Current imaging Cherenkov telescopes.** At their ultimate sensitivity, H.E.S.S.-like instruments leave the higgsino "out of reach by at least a factor of a few". The dominant systematic is the dark-matter density in the inner Galaxy (arXiv:2210.03140).
- **H.E.S.S. Inner Galaxy Survey.** This 2026-dated, unverified paper used 546 h of data (arXiv:2608.07234). It quotes a line limit of 2.3×10⁻²⁸ cm³/s at 1 TeV for an Einasto profile and says the thermal higgsino is "probed" for the first time. Its abstract does not say whether, or for which profiles, the higgsino is excluded.
- **MAGIC.** No MAGIC-specific limit surfaced.
- **Future instruments.**
  - CTA could be the first experiment with sensitivity to the thermal higgsino (arXiv:2008.00692).
  - CTA and SWGO could detect it "at high significance" for all but the most pessimistic profiles (arXiv:2405.13104).
  - CTAO-North could reach the required sensitivity within a decade (arXiv:2506.08084).

The predicted line cross section at 1.1 TeV, and its ratio to current limits, could not be extracted.

### Literature verification status

Every arXiv-API-backed tool failed: metadata lookup, both download tools, and the metadata check inside the citation tool. They returned "not found", HTTP 429 or timeouts, even for the Planck 2018 parameters paper (1807.06209). No quote could be validated and no bibliography entry was made.

Abstract-level text was obtained through OpenAlex for:
- the LZ result (arXiv:2609.02823);
- arXiv:2403.19598;
- arXiv:2410.15733;
- arXiv:2607.20588;
- arXiv:2410.17137.

Planck overview and likelihood papers (1807.06205, 1907.12875) were found. The parameters abstract was not, so Ω_c h² = 0.120 ± 0.001 is used here as the standard value but remains unquoted.

## Discussion

Answering "where does the higgsino sit?" requires assembling three pieces.

**First, the relic target.** This is set by the literature at about 1.1 TeV, give or take about 0.1 TeV. The tool's crossing at about 1158 GeV is consistent with that only because the tool is calibrated there.

**Second, inelastic direct detection.** The xenon kinematics are robust and do not depend on the toy model. At the thermal mass, δ_max is about 368–385 keV depending on the velocity cutoff, nearly independent of mass. The sub-MeV LZ interpretation therefore requires a splitting in a narrow band just below this edge. In the tool, that band is 352–356 keV for one to 0.3 events, and lower splittings are grossly excluded.

The solar-capture bound reported in the literature (delta > 566 keV, or 0.51–0.56 MeV) lies far above this edge under the Standard Halo Model. It also lies above the roughly 480–520 keV LMC-tail values. This is why the LZ interpretation is disfavoured while the higgsino itself survives at delta of order an MeV (arXiv:2610.00226). In that regime, inelastic scattering is closed in xenon. The elastic rate is described as below the neutrino floor, although no number was sourced here.

**Third, indirect detection.** The literature consensus from abstracts is that the higgsino is within an order-one factor of current Fermi-LAT line sensitivity and is not excluded, with strong dependence on the halo profile. CTAO is the decisive future test.

The results agree with the literature on:
- the location of the xenon edge;
- the roughly 350 keV preferred splitting under a Standard-Halo-like cutoff.

They are in tension, or at least unreconciled, with:
- the 377 keV fit of arXiv:2609.02608, where 5–8 keV is unexplained even after the assumed cutoff correction;
- the 339 keV sideband optimum, which is not a comparable quantity.

Dead ends:

- **Verbatim citations.** Verbatim citation of Planck 2018 VI, arXiv:2410.15733, arXiv:2609.02823 and arXiv:2609.02775 was tried twice. Each time, the arXiv API layer returned "not found", 429 errors or internal errors, even for long-established papers. A "not found" result therefore says nothing about whether a paper exists.
- **Tool-based Sommerfeld, halo and indirect-detection studies.** These were impossible because the server has no Sommerfeld switch and no halo parameters, and its indirect-detection model is p-wave.

## Limitations

- **Relic model.** The relic calculation is a toy single-channel scaling. No Sommerfeld or coannihilation physics was computed, and no tool for it was available.
- **Halo model.** Recoil predictions use a single hard 776 km/s cutoff. Halo sensitivity, including v0, v_esc, a smooth tail and the LMC, was only estimated by an analytic rescaling. The Standard Halo Model v0 scan of arXiv:2609.15321 and the sideband analysis of arXiv:2609.26698 were not reproduced.
- **Binned counts.** Counts in the [14,225), [225,271] and (271,800] keV bins were not obtained. The tool returns integrated rates only.
- **Constraint checker.** Its relic pass flag and its indirect-detection model are unreliable. Its viability counts and "no Fermi-LAT exclusion" verdicts should be disregarded.
